Assume full AC. Let $F_0,F_1\subset S^3$ be compact smooth embedded surfaces with the same nonempty boundary link $L$, no closed components, and supplied radial collars. Suppose their entire intersection is $L$ together with $n$ pairwise disjoint isolated smooth arcs $A_j$ with distinct endpoints on $L$. Each is the radial extension of a proper transverse common arc in the link exterior, and the two transverse boundary-curve crossings at its ends have equal ordered signs on the boundary tori oriented outward toward the exterior. No intersection circles occur. Suppose $c(F_0)=c(F_1)=p$ and $n=\operatorname{rank}H_1(F_0;\mathbb Z)+\operatorname{rank}H_1(F_1;\mathbb Z)$.

For every open neighborhood $N$ of $L\cup\bigcup_j A_j$ there is a continuous surjection $Q:S^3\to S^3$, fixed off $N$, whose only nonsingleton fibers are exactly the $A_j$, such that $Q(F_0\cup F_1)$ is a disjoint union of exactly $p$ smooth embedded two-spheres. Each sphere contains the images of exactly one component of each $F_i$. The assertion allows disconnected or nonorientable spanning surfaces and an empty arc list. It does not assert that $Q$ is smooth, recover an alternating diagram, or identify the quotient graph $Q(L)$ with the original link.

Assume full AC. Let $F_0,F_1\subset S^3$ be compact smooth embedded surfaces with the same nonempty boundary link $L$, with no closed components and with supplied radial collars around $L$. Suppose their entire intersection is $L$ together with $n$ pairwise disjoint smooth arcs $A_1,\ldots,A_n$ whose distinct endpoints lie on $L$. Each arc is the isolated radial extension of a proper transverse common arc in the link exterior; the two boundary curves on the surrounding tori cross transversely at its endpoints, with equal ordered intersection signs when the tori are oriented outward toward the exterior. Thus every arc is standard. No intersection circles occur.

Write $b_i=\operatorname{rank}H_1(F_i;\mathbb Z)$ and suppose $c(F_0)=c(F_1)=p$ and $n=b_0+b_1$. There is a continuous surjection $q:S^3\to S^3$ whose only nonsingleton fibers are exactly the arcs $A_j$, supported in any prescribed disjoint neighborhoods of those arcs. Its image $S=q(F_0\cup F_1)$ is a disjoint union of exactly $p$ locally flat embedded topological two-spheres. Each component of $S$ contains the images of exactly one component of each $F_i$. The conclusion includes $n=0$ and allows nonorientable or disconnected spanning surfaces. It does not assert smoothness of these quotient spheres or reconstruct a link diagram.

Assume countable choice. Let $L\subset S^3$ be a smooth link with chosen disjoint smooth normal tubes, and let $F_0,F_1$ be smooth embedded spanning surfaces with boundary $L$. Orient each component of $L$ arbitrarily. Supply radial collar coordinates in the tubes in which each surface collar is given by a smooth ray direction depending on the boundary parameter. Put $X=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}\nu L$, and orient each torus of $\partial\nu L$ as the boundary of the oriented solid tube, so its outward normal points into $X$. Orient the two surface boundary curves on those tori compatibly with $L$.

Let $\alpha$ be a smoothly and properly embedded arc of transverse intersection of $F_0\cap X$ and $F_1\cap X$, transverse to $\partial X$, with transverse boundary-curve crossings at its distinct endpoints. Extend it radially through the supplied collars to the corresponding points of $L$, obtaining a smooth embedded arc $A$. Assume a neighborhood of this extended arc contains no other intersection components. Write $i_0,i_1\in\{1,-1\}$ for the ordered local intersection signs of the two boundary curves at its endpoints, measured on $\partial\nu L$.

The union $F_0\cup F_1$ has a closed intrinsic neighborhood $K$ of $A$ modeled by four pages with common arc, glued at each end by one of the matchings $M=(01)(23)$ and $N=(03)(12)$, with pages zero and two on $F_0$ and pages one and three on $F_1$. The two end matchings differ if and only if $i_0=i_1$. Consequently collapsing $A$ in this neighborhood gives a closed topological disk exactly when $i_0+i_1=2$ or $-2$. When $i_0+i_1=0$ it gives two disks joined at their interior centers. For the standard cases the ambient arc-collapse map can be chosen supported in any prescribed neighborhood of $A$, and its image of $K$ is an embedded topological disk. Local flatness of that disk is not asserted here.

Take four rectangles $P_j=[0,1]_t\times[0,1]_r$, $j\in\{0,1,2,3\}$. Identify their edges $r=0$ pointwise in the $t$ coordinate to a common arc $A$. At each end $t=e$, $e\in\{0,1\}$, also identify the radial edges pointwise in $r$ by a matching $\mu_e$, where each $\mu_e$ is one of $M=(01)(23)$ and $N=(03)(12)$. Let $K$ be this finite quotient complex, and let $C$ be the image of the four outer edges $r=1$.

If the two end matchings differ, then $K/A$ is a closed topological disk whose boundary is exactly the image of $C$, and the collapsed arc is an interior point of that disk. If the two end matchings agree, then $K/A$ is two closed disks joined at their interior centers, so it is not a topological two-manifold at the collapsed point. Explicitly, $K/A$ is the cone on the graph $C$; the latter is one four-edge circle for distinct matchings and two disjoint two-edge circles for equal matchings.

Consequently, if a finite Hausdorff two-dimensional cell complex is already a topological two-manifold away from finitely many disjoint arc subcomplexes, with neighborhoods modeled by the interiors $r<1$ of these four-page models with distinct end matchings, collapsing those arcs gives a topological two-manifold. No boundary is created at a collapsed point. Collapsing any finite disjoint arc subcomplexes preserves the Euler characteristic, whether or not the local end matchings differ. These are intrinsic topological conclusions; an ambient embedding or local flatness needs separate data.

For every CW complex $X$, abelian group $G$, and $n\geq0$, the cellular complex has an
isomorphism $H_n^{\mathrm{cell}}(X;G)\cong H_n(X;G)$, natural with respect to
cellular maps.

For $n\ge1$, $\widetilde H_k(S^n;G)$ is $G$ for $k=n$ and $0$ otherwise.
For $S^0$, $\widetilde H_0(S^0;G)\cong G$ and all other reduced groups vanish.
Thus $H_0(S^n;G)\cong G$ for $n\ge1$, whereas
$H_0(S^0;G)\cong G\oplus G$.

derivations.claim: The restriction of $Q$ to $L$ identifies precisely each pair of endpoints of $A_j$. There are no other identifications, because the whole nonsingleton fibers are exactly the disjoint arcs and their interiors miss $L$. Subdivide $L$ at these finitely many endpoints, adding a vertex on a circle with no endpoints for its cell presentation. Its quotient identifies the two distinct endpoints of each arc to one vertex and retains every open edge. Each such vertex has four incident half-edges, two from each original link point, with loops counted twice. The compact quotient maps continuously and bijectively onto Hausdorff $G$, so is a homeomorphism. It is therefore a finite topological graph, with the additional subdivision vertices on vertex-free circles understood as auxiliary.

In the four-page neighborhood [F2], the image of $L$ is exactly the four radial seams: the common arc is the cone center, and the two short boundary intervals at its endpoints give the four rays. Opposite matchings make the outer graph one circle. Its four page edges alternate between the two surfaces, since every successive endpoint identification joins one page from each surface. The coning chart therefore gives a disk with four radial graph arms and alternating surface sectors. At an uncollapsed boundary point the distinct radial collars give the line chart by angular straightening of their two rays. Any two ambient quotient maps with the same arc fibers differ by an ambient homeomorphism: both factor through the same compact quotient, and the induced continuous bijection of Hausdorff compact targets is a homeomorphism. Hence these actual local marked charts transfer to the specified $Q$, including when its later cap maps have not preserved smooth marked curves.

Fix one sphere component $S_a$ and put $X_i=Q(F_i)\cap S_a$, $G_a=G\cap S_a$. Each $X_i$ is connected, being the image of its one original connected surface component. The intersection $X_0\cap X_1$ equals $G_a$: an equality of image points from the two surfaces is either their original common boundary point or a collapsed common arc, whose image also belongs to $Q(L)$. Use the finite CW structure in [F1] and transport it to this quotient as in step 2.1. Then $X_0,X_1,G_a$ are subcomplexes covering $S_a$. The intersection is nonempty, since every original component has a nonempty boundary circle. Their one-skeleta are connected: attaching a cell of dimension at least two cannot join components of a one-skeleton, as its boundary sphere is connected. Thus for any vertices $u,v$ of $G_a$, there are finite integral cellular one-chains $a\in C_1(X_0)$ and $b\in C_1(X_1)$ with $\partial a=\partial b=v-u$.

The chain $a-b$ is a cellular one-cycle in $S_a$. By [F3] it bounds a cellular two-chain $c$. Split $c=c_0+c_1$ by assigning each of its two-cells to a containing $X_i$, assigning common cells to either side. Then $w=a-\partial c_0=b+\partial c_1$ is a one-chain lying in both cellular chain subgroups, hence in $C_1(G_a)$, and $\partial w=v-u$. If $u,v$ belonged to different graph components, the augmentation counting vertices in the component of $u$ would vanish on every graph edge boundary and hence on $\partial w$, but have value $-1$ on $v-u$. This contradiction proves that all graph vertices lie in one component. Every nonempty finite graph component has a vertex in the chosen cell structure, so $G_a$ is connected.

Finally the two closed subcomplexes $X_i$ cover $S_a$ and intersect exactly in $G_a$. In its complement, the sets $X_i\setminus G_a$ are disjoint, relatively closed and also relatively open because each is the other's complement. Thus a connected complementary component lies wholly in exactly one of them. The line and four-arm charts from step 2.1 give the asserted local colored sectors. Repeating the argument on the finitely many spheres proves all conclusions; when a sphere has no arc vertex its connected finite graph is a single original boundary circle. No crossing height or regularity of marked edges beyond these topological charts has been claimed.

boundaries.reason: The common boundary link is nonempty, every original surface component has boundary, and each sphere contains one component from each side.

boundaries.evidence: Step 5.1 includes a sphere with no arc vertices, whose connected marked graph is a single circle.
Step 4.1 proves connectivity on each individual sphere, allowing p=1 or one arc vertex with loop edges.
Step 1.1 counts a loop twice at a valence-four vertex and retains auxiliary vertices on vertex-free circles.
Step 2.1 uses the actual opposite page matchings and marks their four radial seams; distinct arc endpoints are required in the Statement.
The Statement inherits full AC from finite surface cellulation and quotient suppliers; Step 4.1 is finite integral cellular algebra.

axioms.use: Full AC is inherited from the balanced surface quotient and its finite cellulation. The finite marked graph, local page calculation and cellular chain argument introduce no additional choice.

risk_review.notes: The cellular chain argument proves connectedness without assuming the intersection connected. The local marked charts are topological and do not claim smooth graph edges or overcrossing data.
